Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 77, verses 1–7:

Surat al-Mursalat is Meccan and has fifty verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By those sent forth successively,﴾ ﴿by those that blow violently,﴾ ﴿by those that scatter widely,﴾ ﴿by those that separate decisively,﴾ ﴿by those that deliver a reminder,﴾ ﴿as an excuse or a warning,﴾ ﴿indeed, what you are promised will surely occur.﴾ ﴿So when the stars are obliterated,﴾ [al-Mursalat: 8] ﴿and when the sky is split open,﴾ [al-Mursalat: 9] ﴿and when the mountains are blown away,﴾ [al-Mursalat: 10] ﴿and when the messengers are brought to their appointed time,﴾ [al-Mursalat: 11] ﴿for what day has it been postponed?﴾ [al-Mursalat: 12] ﴿For the Day of Decision.﴾ [al-Mursalat: 13] ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Decision is?﴾ [al-Mursalat: 14] ﴿Woe, that Day, to the deniers!﴾ [al-Mursalat: 15] ﴿Did We not destroy the former peoples?﴾ [al-Mursalat: 16] ﴿Then We follow them with the later ones.﴾ [al-Mursalat: 17] ﴿Thus do We deal with the criminals.﴾ [al-Mursalat: 18] ﴿Woe, that Day, to the deniers!﴾ [al-Mursalat: 19] ﴿Did We not create you from a despised fluid?﴾ [al-Mursalat: 20] ﴿Then We placed it in a secure place,﴾ [al-Mursalat: 21] ﴿for a known term.﴾ [al-Mursalat: 22] ﴿So We determined, and excellent are the determiners.﴾ [al-Mursalat: 23] ﴿Woe, that Day, to the deniers!﴾ [al-Mursalat: 24] ﴿Did We not make the earth a receptacle,﴾ [al-Mursalat: 25] ﴿for the living and the dead?﴾ [al-Mursalat: 26] ﴿And We placed in it firm, towering mountains and gave you sweet water to drink.﴾ [al-Mursalat: 27] ﴿Woe, that Day, to the deniers!﴾ [al-Mursalat: 28]

Commentary: Verses 1 to 28 are quoted in full above.

Faraja al-shay' (I opened the thing): I opened it, and it opened up (infarraja). The rajiz (a poet of the rajaz meter) said:

"The openers of the gate of the unnamed Amir"

Kafata (he gathered and drew together): he gathered and combined. From this is his, upon him be prayers and peace, saying: "Gather (ikfituu) your children." From this the name was given to Baqi' al-Gharqad, and it is called "Kafat" and "Kafatah." Al-kifat (the receptacle) is a noun for that which is gathered, like al-dimam and al-jimah. It is said: "This chapter is the gathering (jimah) of the chapters." Al-Samsama ibn al-Tirimah said:

"Today you are alive upon the earth,
and tomorrow you will be held in a kifat."

Abu 'Ubayda said: al-kifat means a container. Shamakha: he rose high. Al-sharar: what flies off from fire scattered in every direction; its singular is sharara. The dialect of Tamim uses sharar with an alif, its singular being sharara. Al-qasr: a large, built house. Al-qasr also means pieces of wood about a cubit long, above and below which (wood) is prepared for winter; its singular is qasrah. Al-qasar, with a fatha on the sad: (p. 403) the necks of camels, palm trees and people; its singular is qasarah. With a kasra on the qaf and fatha on the sad it is the plural of qasrah, like halqah (ring) of iron and halaq. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

Verses 1 to 28 are quoted in full above.

This surah is Meccan. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and Muqatil that there is one Medinan verse in it, which is: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down.﴾ [al-Mursalat: 48]

Its connection to what precedes is very clear. He, the Exalted, has mercy on whom He wills and punishes the wrongdoers. This is a true promise from Him, so He swore an oath to its occurrence in this (surah), saying: ﴿Indeed, what you are promised will surely occur.﴾

Since the things sworn by are described attributes (mawsufat) that have been omitted, and their attributes have been placed in their stead, there is disagreement about identifying those described things. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah, Abu Salih, Muqatil and al-Farra' said: "those sent forth" (al-mursalat) are the angels, sent with 'urf (kindness), the opposite of nukr (rejection), which is revelation. Thus (they are sent) in succession to the servants, (covering) both ends of the day. Ibn 'Abbas and a group said: they are the prophets (p. 404).

The meaning of 'urfan is: as a bounty from Allah the Exalted to His servants. From this is the poet's saying:

"Kindness does not vanish between Allah and the people."

Its accusative case is because it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu, the accusative of cause): meaning, they were sent for benevolence and kindness. Or (it means) in succession, by analogy with the 'urf (mane) of a horse in the succession of its hair, and the manes of horses. The Arabs say: "The people towards so-and-so are one 'urf" when they head to him in succession, and they are upon him like the 'urf of the hyena when they gather against him. Its accusative case is as a circumstantial accusative (hal). Ibn Mas'ud also said, Ibn 'Abbas also said, and Mujahid and Qatadah said: they are the winds. Al-Hasan said: they are the clouds. The majority read 'urfan with a sukun on the ra'; 'Isa read it with a damma.

Al-'asifat: Ibn Mas'ud said: those that blow with intense gusts. It has been said: the angels drive the souls of the disbelievers violently, that is, they urge them with intensity, or they rush forward as the winds rush, in fulfilling His command. It has been said: they are the destructive signs, such as earthquakes, thunderbolts and eclipses.

Al-nashirat: al-Suddi, Abu Salih and Muqatil said: the angels spread out the records of the servants with their deeds. Al-Rabi' said: the angels raise people from their graves. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatadah said: the winds spread Allah's mercy and His rain. Abu Salih said: the rains give life to the earth with vegetation. Al-Dahhak said: the scrolls are spread before Allah the Exalted with the deeds of the servants. According to this, al-nashirat is in the sense of a relative noun (nasab), meaning: those possessing spreading.

Al-fariqat: Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Salih, Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: the angels distinguish between truth and falsehood, and between the lawful and the unlawful. Qatadah, al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan said: the verses of the Qur'an separated the lawful from the unlawful. Mujahid also said: the winds separate the clouds and scatter them. It has been said: they are the messengers, related by al-Zajjaj. It has been said: the rain-bearing clouds, by analogy with the she-camel al-furuq, which is a pregnant (she-camel) that cries out when she gives birth. It has been said: the intellects distinguish between truth and falsehood, and between the sound and the corrupt.

Al-mulqiyat dhikran: Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and the majority said: the angels deliver what they carry of revelation to the prophets, upon them be prayers and peace. Qutrub said: the messengers deliver what was sent down to them to the nations. Al-Rabi' said: the verses of the Qur'an were cast upon the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Zamakhshari chose from among the opinions that "those sent forth" and the subsequent attributes are either for the angels or for the winds. If for the angels, then "an excuse for the sincere or a warning for the falsifiers." If for the winds, the meaning is: they then deliver a reminder, either as an excuse for those who make excuse to Allah the Exalted by their repentance and seeking forgiveness, when they see Allah's blessing in the rain and give thanks for it, or as a warning for those who are heedless of thanking Allah and attribute that to the weather-stars (anwa'). They are described as "delivering the reminder" because they are a cause of its occurrence, when the blessing is thanked for through them, or disbelieved in. This is what al-Zamakhshari said. What I consider correct is that the thing sworn by is two things, and for this reason the conjunction with waw (and) came in "al-nashirat." The conjunction with waw indicates difference; indeed, that is its established function in the Arabic language. As for the conjunction with fa' (then) when it is among the attributes, it indicates that they refer back to al-'adiyat (the chargers), which are horses, as in his saying:

"O, the grief of Zaybah for al-Harith, then the one who dawns, then the one who seizes spoils, then the one who returns."

Here they refer back to a single described thing, which is al-Harith. Having established this, the apparent meaning is that He first swore by the winds, which are His sent ones, and this is shown by the attribute being joined by fa' as we have said, and that blowing violently is an attribute of the wind in several places in the Qur'an. The second category includes an ascent to something more noble than the first thing sworn by, namely the angels, and al-fariqat and al-mulqiyat are among their attributes, as we have said regarding the conjunction of attributes. Their delivering the reminder, which is what Allah sent down, may validly be ascribed to them. The majority read al-mulqiyat as an active participle, lightened, meaning: we bring it to them. Ibn 'Abbas read it with shaddah from al-talqiyah, which is also conveying speech to the addressee. It is said: "I made him receive the reminder, and he received it." Ibn 'Abbas also read it, as al-Mahdawi reported, with a fatha on the lam and the qaf with shaddah, as a passive participle, meaning: it received it from Allah the Exalted.

Ibrahim al-Taymi, the two grammarians (al-Nahwiyyan, i.e., Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i) and Hafs read "'udhran aw nudhran" with sukun on both dhal sounds. Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn Kharijah, Talhah, Abu Ja'far, Abu Haywah, 'Isa, al-Hasan (with variant), al-A'sha from Abu Bakr read both with damma. Abu Ja'far also, Shaybah, Zayd ibn 'Ali, the two Haramis (Makkan and Madinan readers), Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read it with sukun in "'udhran" and damma in "nudhran." The sukun reading is that both are verbal nouns (masadir), singular, or plural verbal nouns. So "'udhran" is the plural of "'adhir" in the sense of excuse, and "nudhran" is the plural of "nadhir" in the sense of warning. Their accusative case is either as a substitution (badal) for "dhikran," as if it were said: "those delivering excuses or warnings," or as an object of purpose, or as two verbal nouns in a circumstantial position, meaning: making excuse or warning. With sukun it is permissible for both to be plurals as we have explained. It has been said that the accusative of "'udhran aw nudhran" is valid as a direct object of the verbal noun which is "dhikran," meaning: "al-mulqiyat," that is, "they mentioned an excuse." This is weak, because the verbal noun here is not intended to function as a verb; it is intended as a reality, by his saying: "Was the reminder cast upon him?" Excuse (i'dhar) is by the establishment of proof upon the creation, and warning (inqh) is by punishment and vengeance.

﴿Indeed, what you are promised﴾: that is, of the recompense of reward and punishment. (Surely occur): "ma" is a relative pronoun, even though it was written joined with "inna." This clause is the thing sworn to. The majority read "aw nudhran" with the conjunction of distinction (aw), and Ibrahim al-Taymi read "wa nudhran" with the conjunction of coordination (wa).

Al-Bahr al-Muhit, Abu Hayyan al-Andalusi, al-Muhit.

Its connection to what precedes is very clear. He, the Exalted, has mercy on whom He wills and punishes the wrongdoers. This is a true promise from Him, so He swore an oath to its occurrence in this (surah), saying: ﴿Indeed, what you are promised will surely occur.﴾

Since the things sworn by are described attributes (mawsufat) that have been omitted, and their attributes have been placed in their stead, there is disagreement about identifying those described things. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah, Abu Salih, Muqatil and al-Farra' said: "those sent forth" (al-mursalat) are the angels, sent with 'urf (kindness), the opposite of nukr (rejection), which is revelation. Thus (they are sent) in succession to the servants, (covering) both ends of the day. Ibn 'Abbas and a group said: they are the prophets (p. 404).

The meaning of 'urfan is: as a bounty from Allah the Exalted to His servants. From this is the poet's saying:

"Kindness does not vanish between Allah and the people."

Its accusative case is because it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu, the accusative of cause): meaning, they were sent for benevolence and kindness. Or (it means) in succession, by analogy with the 'urf (mane) of a horse in the succession of its hair, and the manes of horses. The Arabs say: "The people towards so-and-so are one 'urf" when they head to him in succession, and they are upon him like the 'urf of the hyena when they gather against him. Its accusative case is as a circumstantial accusative (hal). Ibn Mas'ud also said, Ibn 'Abbas also said, and Mujahid and Qatadah said: they are the winds. Al-Hasan said: they are the clouds. The majority read 'urfan with a sukun on the ra'; 'Isa read it with a damma.

Al-'asifat: Ibn Mas'ud said: those that blow with intense gusts. It has been said: the angels drive the souls of the disbelievers violently, that is, they urge them with intensity, or they rush forward as the winds rush, in fulfilling His command. It has been said: they are the destructive signs, such as earthquakes, thunderbolts and eclipses.

Al-nashirat: al-Suddi, Abu Salih and Muqatil said: the angels spread out the records of the servants with their deeds. Al-Rabi' said: the angels raise people from their graves. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatadah said: the winds spread Allah's mercy and His rain. Abu Salih said: the rains give life to the earth with vegetation. Al-Dahhak said: the scrolls are spread before Allah the Exalted with the deeds of the servants. According to this, al-nashirat is in the sense of a relative noun (nasab), meaning: those possessing spreading.

Al-fariqat: Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Salih, Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: the angels distinguish between truth and falsehood, and between the lawful and the unlawful. Qatadah, al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan said: the verses of the Qur'an separated the lawful from the unlawful. Mujahid also said: the winds separate the clouds and scatter them. It has been said: they are the messengers, related by al-Zajjaj. It has been said: the rain-bearing clouds, by analogy with the she-camel al-furuq, which is a pregnant (she-camel) that cries out when she gives birth. It has been said: the intellects distinguish between truth and falsehood, and between the sound and the corrupt.

Al-mulqiyat dhikran: Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and the majority said: the angels deliver what they carry of revelation to the prophets, upon them be prayers and peace. Qutrub said: the messengers deliver what was sent down to them to the nations. Al-Rabi' said: the verses of the Qur'an were cast upon the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Zamakhshari chose from among the opinions that "those sent forth" and the subsequent attributes are either for the angels or for the winds. If for the angels, then "an excuse for the sincere or a warning for the falsifiers." If for the winds, the meaning is: they then deliver a reminder, either as an excuse for those who make excuse to Allah the Exalted by their repentance and seeking forgiveness, when they see Allah's blessing in the rain and give thanks for it, or as a warning for those who are heedless of thanking Allah and attribute that to the weather-stars (anwa'). They are described as "delivering the reminder" because they are a cause of its occurrence, when the blessing is thanked for through them, or disbelieved in. This is what al-Zamakhshari said. What I consider correct is that the thing sworn by is two things, and for this reason the conjunction with waw (and) came in "al-nashirat." The conjunction with waw indicates difference; indeed, that is its established function in the Arabic language. As for the conjunction with fa' (then) when it is among the attributes, it indicates that they refer back to al-'adiyat (the chargers), which are horses, as in his saying:

"O, the grief of Zaybah for al-Harith, then the one who dawns, then the one who seizes spoils, then the one who returns."

Here they refer back to a single described thing, which is al-Harith. Having established this, the apparent meaning is that He first swore by the winds, which are His sent ones, and this is shown by the attribute being joined by fa' as we have said, and that blowing violently is an attribute of the wind in several places in the Qur'an. The second category includes an ascent to something more noble than the first thing sworn by, namely the angels, and al-fariqat and al-mulqiyat are among their attributes, as we have said regarding the conjunction of attributes. Their delivering the reminder, which is what Allah sent down, may validly be ascribed to them. The majority read al-mulqiyat as an active participle, lightened, meaning: we bring it to them. Ibn 'Abbas read it with shaddah from al-talqiyah, which is also conveying speech to the addressee. It is said: "I made him receive the reminder, and he received it." Ibn 'Abbas also read it, as al-Mahdawi reported, with a fatha on the lam and the qaf with shaddah, as a passive participle, meaning: it received it from Allah the Exalted.

Their accusative case is either as a substitution (badal) for "dhikran," as if it were said: "those delivering excuses or warnings," or as an object of purpose, or as two verbal nouns in a circumstantial position, meaning: making excuse or warning. Excuse (i'dhar) is by the establishment of proof upon the creation, and warning (inqh) is by punishment and vengeance.

﴿إلى قَدَرٍ مَعْلُومٍ﴾: that is, with Allah, exalted is He, and it is the time of birth.

ʿAlī ibn Abi Ṭālib read *fa-qaddarnā* with a doubled *dāl*, from *taqdīr* (determination), as He said: ﴿مِن نُطْفَةٍ خَلَقَهُ فَقَدَّرَهُ﴾ [ʿAbasa: 19]. The rest of the seven read it with a lightened *dāl*, from *al-qudra* (power).

﴿أحْياءً وأمْواتًا﴾ is in the accusative by a verb indicated by what precedes it, that is: He gathers (*yaknitu*) the living upon its surface and the dead in its belly. From this, whoever says that the grave-robber (*al-nabbāsh*) has his hand cut off uses it as evidence, because the belly of the earth is the safe-keeping (*ḥirz*) of the shroud, so when he digs it up and takes from it, he is a thief.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: It is possible that the meaning is: We gather you, living and dead, and they are in the accusative as circumstantial states (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun, because it is known that the earth is the gatherer of mankind. He finished.

*Rawāsiya*: firm mountains.

﴿شامِخاتٍ﴾: lofty, elevated. From it comes *shamakha bi-anfihi*: he raised, he became high. He likened the meaning to the body.

*Wa-asqaynākum*: We made it a source of watering for your crops and your benefits.

﴿فَإذا النُّجُومُ طُمِسَتْ﴾: that is, its light is removed and it becomes level with the body of the sky. Or it is an expression for the extinguishing of its essence, which is its scattering and dimming. Or its light is removed and then it is scattered, its light erased.

﴿وإذا السَّماءُ فُرِجَتْ﴾: that is, it will have openings in it through being split apart. ʿAmr ibn Maymun read *ṭummisat* and *furrijat* with a doubled *mīm* and *rāʾ*, while the majority read them with single letters.

﴿وإذا الجِبالُ نُسِفَتْ﴾: that is, the winds scatter them. This happens after they are set in motion and before they become scattered dust (*habāʾ*). The majority read *uqqitat* with a *hamza* and a doubled *qāf*. Al-Nakhaʿī, al-Ḥasan, ʿĪsā and Khālid read it with a lightened *qāf* and *hamza*. Abu al-Ashhab, ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, ʿĪsā also, and Abu ʿAmr read it with a *wāw* and a doubled *qāf*. ʿĪsā said: "This is the dialect of Lower Muḍar." ʿAbd Allāh (Ibn Masʿūd), al-Ḥasan and Abu Jaʿfar read it with a single *wāw* and a lightened *qāf*. Al-Ḥasan also read *wuwiqat* with two *wāws* on the pattern *fūʿilat*. The meaning is: a set appointed time was made for it, and it arrived and came; or it reached the appointed time for which it was waiting, which is the Day of Resurrection. The *wāw* is the original in all of this and the *hamza* is a substitute. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the meaning of the appointment of the Messengers is the specifying of the time at which they attend to bear witness against their nations. The answer to *idhā* (when) is omitted, since what precedes it indicates it, and its estimated form is: "When such and such occurs, what you are promised will come to pass."

﴿لِأيِّ يَوْمٍ أُجِّلَتْ﴾: this is an exaltation of that day and an expression of wonder at the terror and severity that occur in it. *Al-taʾjīl* is from *al-ajal* (term), that is: for a great day they were delayed.

﴿لِيَوْمِ الفَصْلِ﴾: that is, between the creatures.

(*Wayl*): the discussion of it has already preceded at the beginning of the second *ḥizb* of Surat al-Baqara.

*Yawmaʾidhin* (on that day): the day when the stars are extinguished, and what follows it occurs.

The majority read ﴿نُهْلِكِ الأوَّلِينَ﴾ with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn*, while Qatada read it with a *fatḥa*. Al-Zamakhsharī said: from *halakahu*, meaning *ahlakahu* (to destroy him). Al-ʿAjjāj said:

*And a wasteland, deadly to whoever ventures into it.*

He finished. Some scholars explained *hālik man taʿarrajā* as follows: *hālik* is intransitive, and *man* is a relative pronoun (*mawṣūl*). Therefore it was used as evidence that the attributive adjective (*al-ṣifa al-mushabbaha*, the adjective resembling the active participle) may have a relative pronoun as its complement.

The majority read ﴿نُتْبِعُهُمُ﴾ with a *ḍamma* on the *ʿayn* as a new sentence (*istiʾnāf*), and it is a promise to the people of Makkah. The reading of ʿAbd Allāh supports the new sentence: *thumma sa-nutbiʿuhum* with the *sīn* of the future. Al-Aʿraj and al-ʿAbbās from Abu ʿAmr read it with a sukun. This may be coordinated with *nuhlik* (*nuhlik* and then *nutbiʿ*), or it may be a sukun for lightening, as *wa-mā yush‘irukum* [al-Anʿām: 109] was given a sukun. It is then a new sentence. According to the new sentence, *al-awwalīn* (the former ones) are the nations who preceded Quraysh altogether, and *al-ākhirīn* (the latter ones) are those who came after Quraysh and others. According to the coordination, *al-awwalīn* are the people of Nuh and Ibrahim, peace be upon them, and those who were with them, and *al-ākhirīn* are the people of Pharaoh and those who came after them and were near the period of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

The destruction here is the destruction of punishment and retribution, and for this reason it came with ﴿كَذَلِكَ نَفْعَلُ بِالمُجْرِمِينَ﴾ (Thus do We deal with the guilty). It brought the attribute that requires the destruction by punishment, which is criminality.

When He mentioned the annihilation of the former and latter ones (p-406), He mentioned and drew attention to the origin of creation, the consideration of which requires the possibility of resurrection.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 77, verse 29–50:

﴿Proceed to that which you used to deny.﴾ ﴿Proceed to a shadow with three branches,﴾ ﴿neither shading nor availing against the blaze.﴾ ﴿Indeed, it throws up sparks like a fortress,﴾ ﴿as if they were yellow camels.﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿This is a day when they will not speak,﴾ ﴿nor will they be permitted to offer excuses.﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿This is the Day of Judgement; We have gathered you and the former peoples.﴾ ﴿So if you have any stratagem, then use it against Me.﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿Indeed, the God-conscious will be amid shades and springs,﴾ ﴿and fruits of what they desire.﴾ ﴿"Eat and drink with satisfaction for what you used to do."﴾ ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿"Eat and enjoy yourselves a little; indeed you are criminals."﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down.﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿So in what statement after this will they believe?﴾

It is said to the deniers: ﴿Proceed to that which you used to deny﴾, i.e., of the punishment. ﴿Proceed to a shadow﴾: an imperative. The reading of the majority is a repetition or an explanation of the destination. Ruways, on the authority of Ya'qub, read it with a fatha on the lam (inflected as a report), meaning: when they were commanded, they complied and set off, since it was not possible for them to delay, having become compelled to set off. ﴿With three branches﴾: 'Ata' said: it is the smoke of Jahannam. It was narrated that it rises from three places, and the disbelievers think that it will shield them from the Fire, so they rush toward it, only to find it in the worst condition. Ibn 'Abbas said: (p-407) it is said this to the worshippers of the cross: the believers are in the shade of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, while they are in the shade of their object of worship, which is the cross, which has three branches. A shi'b is that which separates from a single body. ﴿Neither shading﴾: a negation of the merits of shade. ﴿Nor availing﴾: i.e., nor will it avail them anything against the heat of the blaze. ﴿Indeed, it throws up sparks﴾: the pronoun in "innaha" refers to Jahannam. The majority read "bi-sharar," while 'Isa read "bi-shirar" with an alif between the two r's, and Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Miqsam likewise but with a kasra on the shin. This may be the plural of sharar, i.e., "with embers of punishment," or it may be an adjective placed in the position of its noun, i.e., "with evil ones of the people," as you say: "qawm shirar," the plural of sharr (not the elative form), and "qawm khiyar," the plural of khayr (not the elative form). This is feminized as "sharrah" and "khayrah" for the feminine, unlike when the two are used as elatives; they have rules mentioned in grammar. The majority read "kal-qasr" (as the fortress). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Hasan, and Ibn Miqsam read it with a fatha on the qaf and the sad. Ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan also read "ka-l-qisar," with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the sad. Some readers read it with a fatha on the qaf and a kasra on the sad. Ibn Mas'ud read it with a damma on both. It is as if it were a shortened form of "qusur" (palaces), just as they shortened "najm" and "namir" from "nujum" and "numur." The rajiz said:

"Therein are lions and leopards."

The explanation of most of these readings has already been given in the vocabulary section. The majority, among them 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), read "jimalat" with a kasra on the jim, with an alif and a ta', the plural of "jimal," which is the plural of jamal (camels). It is like their saying "rijalat Quraysh." Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, and Abu Raja', with a variant from them, read it the same way, except that they put a damma on the jim, and it means the ropes of ships. One unit of these is "jumlah," since it is a bundle (jumlah) of strengths and powers. Then it was pluralized as "jumal" and "jimal," then "jumal" was pluralized again as a sound plural, so they said "jumalat." It was also said: "jimalat" means the large cables of bridges. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, Abu 'Amr in the narration of al-Asma'i, and Harun on his authority read "jimalah" with a kasra on the jim, the ta' being attached to "jimal" to feminize the collective noun, like "hajar" and "hijarah." Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sulami, al-A'mash, Abu Haywah, Abu Bahriyyah, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, and Ruways read likewise, except that they put a damma on the jim. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: "jimalat" are the large ropes of ships, which are their great cables; when they gather round, one against another, large masses result. Ibn 'Abbas also said: "jimalat" are large pieces of copper, and the derivation of these is from the name "jumlah." Al-Hasan read "sufr" with a damma on the fa', while the majority read it with a sukun. It likened the sparks first to the fortress, which is the castle in terms of size and in terms of height in the air, and second to camels, to clarify the comparison. Do you not see that they liken camels to large jars, which are palaces? The poet said:

"I halted there with my she-camel, and she was like a jar, so that I might fulfill the need of the one who lingers."

Whoever reads with a damma on the jim, the comparison is in terms of size and height. Bright yellow is more similar to the color of sparks. The majority said so. It was also said: "sufr sud" (yellowish-black), and it was said: "sud" inclining toward yellow. 'Imran ibn Hittan al-Raqashi said:

"They called to them with the highest of their voices and cast at them, like the camels of yellow color, that tear the skin."

Al-A'mash, al-A'raj, Zayd ibn 'Ali, 'Isa, Abu Haywah, and 'Asim in one narration read ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾ with a fatha on the mim, while the majority read it with a damma. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: when it is attached to a non-declinable noun, it is built, so the vowel is a building vowel, and it is in the position of a nominative. The author of al-Lawami' said: 'Isa said it is the dialect of lower Mudar, meaning that they built "yawm" with "la" on the fatha, because they made "yawm ma' la" like a single word, so it is in the position of the nominative, since it is the predicate of the subject. End. The sentence introduced by a present-tense verb, whether affirmative or negated, the Basrans do not allow building the adverb attached to it in any way; this is only a Kufan doctrine. The author of al-Lawami' said: it may also be a correct accusative as an adverb, so that this becomes a reference to what preceded in the speech, not a reference to "yawm," and the operator governing the accusative of "yawm" would be a call preceded by a description of (p-408) Jahannam and its throwing of sparks, in "the day when they will not speak," so "yawma'idhin" becomes an intervening clause that does not prevent the freeing of the operator for its object, just as in ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 47] ﴿Both having branches﴾ [al-Rahman: 48]. End. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it may also be an adverb, and the reference by "this" is to its throwing of sparks. al-Zamakhshari said: al-A'mash put it in the accusative, meaning: this which has been related to you occurs on that day. Here there is a negation of their speech, while Allah has informed us that they spoke at places during this day, and this is in consideration of the length of the day, so it is valid to negate speech in it at one time and affirm it at another, or the negation refers to speech with a proof that benefits, and their speech with what does not benefit is treated as no speech at all.

All the readers, as far as I know, read ﴿wa-la yu'dhanu﴾ in the passive. Abu 'Ali al-Ahwazi related that Zayd ibn 'Ali read "wa-la ya'dhanu" in the active, meaning Allah, Exalted is He. ﴿fa-ya'taddhirun﴾: it is conjoined to ﴿wa-la yu'dhanu﴾ and falls within the scope of the negation of permission, meaning: there is no permission, so there is no excuse-making, and he did not make the excuse-making a consequence of permission, so that it would be put in the subjunctive. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it was not put in the subjunctive after the negation because of the similarity of the verse-endings, and both readings are permissible. End. Thus he made the refusal of the subjunctive the similarity of verse-endings, and said both readings are permissible, and it appears from his words that the nominative and subjunctive are equal and their meaning is one. This is not so, because the nominative, as we mentioned, is not a consequence but a clear conjunction, while the subjunctive makes it a consequence, so they differ. Abu al-Hajjaj al-A'lam held that a verb may be nominative while its meaning is that of the subjunctive after the fa', and this is rare. The grammarians only made the meaning of the nominative different from that of the subjunctive out of consideration for the majority of Arabic usage, and took this as their evidence. This verse is like the apparent sense of Ibn 'Atiyyah's words, and Ibn 'Usfur and others have refuted this.

﴿This is the Day of Judgement; We have gathered you﴾ — to the disbelievers — ﴿and the former peoples﴾: the people of Nuh, peace be upon him, and the other disbelievers whose time preceded the time of those addressed, i.e., We have gathered you for the separation between the happy and the wretched. ﴿So if you have any stratagem﴾: i.e., on this day, just as you had in the world schemes by which you plotted against the religion of Allah and His friends. ﴿Then use it against Me﴾ today. This is a challenge to them and a rebuke. Since Surat al-Insan mentioned briefly some of the conditions of the disbelievers in the Hereafter and expanded on the description of the conditions of the believers there, this surah expands on the description of the disbelievers and is brief on the description of the believers, so that a balance was achieved between the two surahs. The majority read ﴿fi zilal﴾ as the plural of zill, while al-A'mash read "fi zulal," the plural of zullah. ﴿Eat and drink﴾: an address to them in the Hereafter, with the saying implied, indicated by ﴿for what you used to do﴾.

﴿Eat and enjoy yourselves﴾: an address to the disbelievers in the world. (A little): i.e., for a little time, since the utmost of your eating and enjoyment is death. It is an address of threat to whoever among Quraysh and others committed crime. ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down"﴾: whoever said this surah is Meccan said it was about Quraysh, and whoever said this verse is Medinan said it was about the hypocrites. Muqatil said: it was revealed about Thaqif, who said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Remove the prayer from us, for we will not bow; it is a disgrace." He refused and said: "There is no good in a religion without prayer." The meaning of "bow down": be humble before Allah and submit to Him by accepting His revelation. It was also said: bowing here is an expression for prayer, and bowing was singled out from its acts because the Arabs used to be disdainful of bowing and prostration. In this surah, after every sentence, comes the statement: ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾, because each sentence in it contains an account by Allah, Exalted is He, of matters of the conditions of the Hereafter and descriptions of matters of the conditions of this world, so it is fitting that we mention the threat after each sentence to the one who denies, with woe on the Day of the Hereafter. The pronoun in "ba'dahu" refers to the Qur'an, and the meaning is that it has contained, in terms of inimitability, eloquence, reports of unseen matters, and other things, what no divine book has contained. So if they deny it, then in what statement after it will they believe? I.e., it is not possible for them to believe any statement after they have denied this statement, which is the Qur'an. The majority read "yu'minun" with the third-person ya', while Ya'qub and Ibn 'Amir in one narration read it with the second-person ta'.

The reading of the majority is a repetition or an explanation of the destination. Ruways, on the authority of Ya'qub, read it with a fatha on the lam (inflected as a report), meaning: when they were commanded, they complied and set off, since it was not possible for them to delay, having become compelled to set off. ﴿With three branches﴾: 'Ata' said: it is the smoke of Jahannam. Ibn 'Abbas said: (p-407) it is said this to the worshippers of the cross: the believers are in the shade of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, while they are in the shade of their object of worship, which is the cross, which has three branches. A shi'b is that which separates from a single body. ﴿Neither shading﴾: a negation of the merits of shade. ﴿Nor availing﴾: i.e., nor will it avail them anything against the heat of the blaze. ﴿Indeed, it throws up sparks﴾: the pronoun in "innaha" refers to Jahannam. The majority read "bi-sharar," while 'Isa read "bi-shirar" with an alif between the two r's, and Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Miqsam likewise but with a kasra on the shin. "Therein are lions and leopards."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 77, verse 29–50:

﴿Proceed to that which you used to deny.﴾ ﴿Proceed to a shadow with three branches,﴾ ﴿neither shading nor availing against the blaze.﴾ ﴿Indeed, it throws up sparks like a fortress,﴾ ﴿as if they were yellow camels.﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿This is a day when they will not speak,﴾ ﴿nor will they be permitted to offer excuses.﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿This is the Day of Judgement; We have gathered you and the former peoples.﴾ ﴿So if you have any stratagem, then use it against Me.﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿Indeed, the God-conscious will be amid shades and springs,﴾ ﴿and fruits of what they desire.﴾ ﴿"Eat and drink with satisfaction for what you used to do."﴾ ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿"Eat and enjoy yourselves a little; indeed you are criminals."﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down.﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿So in what statement after this will they believe?﴾

It is said to the deniers: ﴿Proceed to that which you used to deny﴾, i.e., of the punishment. ﴿Proceed to a shadow﴾: an imperative. The reading of the majority is a repetition or an explanation of the destination. Ruways, on the authority of Ya'qub, read it with a fatha on the lam (inflected as a report), meaning: when they were commanded, they complied and set off, since it was not possible for them to delay, having become compelled to set off. ﴿With three branches﴾: 'Ata' said: it is the smoke of Jahannam. It was narrated that it rises from three places, and the disbelievers think that it will shield them from the Fire, so they rush toward it, only to find it in the worst condition. Ibn 'Abbas said: (p-407) it is said this to the worshippers of the cross: the believers are in the shade of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, while they are in the shade of their object of worship, which is the cross, which has three branches. A shi'b is that which separates from a single body. ﴿Neither shading﴾: a negation of the merits of shade. ﴿Nor availing﴾: i.e., nor will it avail them anything against the heat of the blaze. ﴿Indeed, it throws up sparks﴾: the pronoun in "innaha" refers to Jahannam. The majority read "bi-sharar," while 'Isa read "bi-shirar" with an alif between the two r's, and Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Miqsam likewise but with a kasra on the shin. This may be the plural of sharar, i.e., "with embers of punishment," or it may be an adjective placed in the position of its noun, i.e., "with evil ones of the people," as you say: "qawm shirar," the plural of sharr (not the elative form), and "qawm khiyar," the plural of khayr (not the elative form). This is feminized as "sharrah" and "khayrah" for the feminine, unlike when the two are used as elatives; they have rules mentioned in grammar. The majority read "kal-qasr" (as the fortress). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Hasan, and Ibn Miqsam read it with a fatha on the qaf and the sad. Ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan also read "ka-l-qisar," with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the sad. Some readers read it with a fatha on the qaf and a kasra on the sad. Ibn Mas'ud read it with a damma on both. It is as if it were a shortened form of "qusur" (palaces), just as they shortened "najm" and "namir" from "nujum" and "numur." The rajiz said:

"Therein are lions and leopards."

The explanation of most of these readings has already been given in the vocabulary section. The majority, among them 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), read "jimalat" with a kasra on the jim, with an alif and a ta', the plural of "jimal," which is the plural of jamal (camels). It is like their saying "rijalat Quraysh." Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, and Abu Raja', with a variant from them, read it the same way, except that they put a damma on the jim, and it means the ropes of ships. One unit of these is "jumlah," since it is a bundle (jumlah) of strengths and powers. Then it was pluralized as "jumal" and "jimal," then "jumal" was pluralized again as a sound plural, so they said "jumalat." It was also said: "jimalat" means the large cables of bridges. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, Abu 'Amr in the narration of al-Asma'i, and Harun on his authority read "jimalah" with a kasra on the jim, the ta' being attached to "jimal" to feminize the collective noun, like "hajar" and "hijarah." Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sulami, al-A'mash, Abu Haywah, Abu Bahriyyah, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, and Ruways read likewise, except that they put a damma on the jim. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: "jimalat" are the large ropes of ships, which are their great cables; when they gather round, one against another, large masses result. Ibn 'Abbas also said: "jimalat" are large pieces of copper, and the derivation of these is from the name "jumlah." Al-Hasan read "sufr" with a damma on the fa', while the majority read it with a sukun. It likened the sparks first to the fortress, which is the castle in terms of size and in terms of height in the air, and second to camels, to clarify the comparison. "They called to them with the highest of their voices and cast at them, like the camels of yellow color, that tear the skin."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 77, verse 29–50:

﴿Proceed to that which you used to deny.﴾ ﴿Proceed to a shadow with three branches,﴾ ﴿neither shading nor availing against the blaze.﴾ ﴿Indeed, it throws up sparks like a fortress,﴾ ﴿as if they were yellow camels.﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿This is a day when they will not speak,﴾ ﴿nor will they be permitted to offer excuses.﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿This is the Day of Judgement; We have gathered you and the former peoples.﴾ ﴿So if you have any stratagem, then use it against Me.﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿Indeed, the God-conscious will be amid shades and springs,﴾ ﴿and fruits of what they desire.﴾ ﴿"Eat and drink with satisfaction for what you used to do."﴾ ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿"Eat and enjoy yourselves a little; indeed you are criminals."﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down.﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿So in what statement after this will they believe?﴾

It is said to the deniers: ﴿Proceed to that which you used to deny﴾, i.e., of the punishment. ﴿Proceed to a shadow﴾: an imperative. The reading of the majority is a repetition or an explanation of the destination. Ruways, on the authority of Ya'qub, read it with a fatha on the lam (inflected as a report), meaning: when they were commanded, they complied and set off, since it was not possible for them to delay, having become compelled to set off. ﴿With three branches﴾: 'Ata' said: it is the smoke of Jahannam. It was narrated that it rises from three places, and the disbelievers think that it will shield them from the Fire, so they rush toward it, only to find it in the worst condition. Ibn 'Abbas said: (p-407) it is said this to the worshippers of the cross: the believers are in the shade of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, while they are in the shade of their object of worship, which is the cross, which has three branches. A shi'b is that which separates from a single body. ﴿Neither shading﴾: a negation of the merits of shade. ﴿Nor availing﴾: i.e., nor will it avail them anything against the heat of the blaze. ﴿Indeed, it throws up sparks﴾: the pronoun in "innaha" refers to Jahannam. The majority read "bi-sharar," while 'Isa read "bi-shirar" with an alif between the two r's, and Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Miqsam likewise but with a kasra on the shin. This may be the plural of sharar, i.e., "with embers of punishment," or it may be an adjective placed in the position of its noun, i.e., "with evil ones of the people," as you say: "qawm shirar," the plural of sharr (not the elative form), and "qawm khiyar," the plural of khayr (not the elative form). This is feminized as "sharrah" and "khayrah" for the feminine, unlike when the two are used as elatives; they have rules mentioned in grammar. The majority read "kal-qasr" (as the fortress). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Hasan, and Ibn Miqsam read it with a fatha on the qaf and the sad. Ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan also read "ka-l-qisar," with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the sad. Some readers read it with a fatha on the qaf and a kasra on the sad. Ibn Mas'ud read it with a damma on both. It is as if it were a shortened form of "qusur" (palaces), just as they shortened "najm" and "namir" from "nujum" and "numur." The rajiz said:

"Therein are lions and leopards."

The explanation of most of these readings has already been given in the vocabulary section. The majority, among them 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), read "jimalat" with a kasra on the jim, with an alif and a ta', the plural of "jimal," which is the plural of jamal (camels). It is like their saying "rijalat Quraysh." Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, and Abu Raja', with a variant from them, read it the same way, except that they put a damma on the jim, and it means the ropes of ships. One unit of these is "jumlah," since it is a bundle (jumlah) of strengths and powers. Then it was pluralized as "jumal" and "jimal," then "jumal" was pluralized again as a sound plural, so they said "jumalat." It was also said: "jimalat" means the large cables of bridges. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, Abu 'Amr in the narration of al-Asma'i, and Harun on his authority read "jimalah" with a kasra on the jim, the ta' being attached to "jimal" to feminize the collective noun, like "hajar" and "hijarah." Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sulami, al-A'mash, Abu Haywah, Abu Bahriyyah, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, and Ruways read likewise, except that they put a damma on the jim. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: "jimalat" are the large ropes of ships, which are their great cables; when they gather round, one against another, large masses result. Ibn 'Abbas also said: "jimalat" are large pieces of copper, and the derivation of these is from the name "jumlah." Al-Hasan read "sufr" with a damma on the fa', while the majority read it with a sukun. It likened the sparks first to the fortress, which is the castle in terms of size and in terms of height in the air, and second to camels, to clarify the comparison. Do you not see that they liken camels to large jars, which are palaces? The poet said:

"I halted there with my she-camel, and she was like a jar, so that I might fulfill the need of the one who lingers."

Whoever reads with a damma on the jim, the comparison is in terms of size and height. Bright yellow is more similar to the color of sparks. The majority said so. It was also said: "sufr sud" (yellowish-black), and it was said: "sud" inclining toward yellow. 'Imran ibn Hittan al-Raqashi said:

"They called to them with the highest of their voices and cast at them, like the camels of yellow color, that tear the skin."

Al-A'mash, al-A'raj, Zayd ibn 'Ali, 'Isa, Abu Haywah, and 'Asim in one narration read ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾ with a fatha on the mim, while the majority read it with a damma. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: when it is attached to a non-declinable noun, it is built, so the vowel is a building vowel, and it is in the position of a nominative. The author of al-Lawami' said: 'Isa said it is the dialect of lower Mudar, meaning that they built "yawm" with "la" on the fatha, because they made "yawm ma' la" like a single word, so it is in the position of the nominative, since it is the predicate of the subject. End. The sentence introduced by a present-tense verb, whether affirmative or negated, the Basrans do not allow building the adverb attached to it in any way; this is only a Kufan doctrine. The author of al-Lawami' said: it may also be a correct accusative as an adverb, so that this becomes a reference to what preceded in the speech, not a reference to "yawm," and the operator governing the accusative of "yawm" would be a call preceded by a description of (p-408) Jahannam and its throwing of sparks, in "the day when they will not speak," so "yawma'idhin" becomes an intervening clause that does not prevent the freeing of the operator for its object, just as in ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 47] ﴿Both having branches﴾ [al-Rahman: 48]. End. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it may also be an adverb, and the reference by "this" is to its throwing of sparks. al-Zamakhshari said: al-A'mash put it in the accusative, meaning: this which has been related to you occurs on that day. Here there is a negation of their speech, while Allah has informed us that they spoke at places during this day, and this is in consideration of the length of the day, so it is valid to negate speech in it at one time and affirm it at another, or the negation refers to speech with a proof that benefits, and their speech with what does not benefit is treated as no speech at all.

All the readers, as far as I know, read ﴿wa-la yu'dhanu﴾ in the passive. Abu 'Ali al-Ahwazi related that Zayd ibn 'Ali read "wa-la ya'dhanu" in the active, meaning Allah, Exalted is He. ﴿fa-ya'taddhirun﴾: it is conjoined to ﴿wa-la yu'dhanu﴾ and falls within the scope of the negation of permission, meaning: there is no permission, so there is no excuse-making, and he did not make the excuse-making a consequence of permission, so that it would be put in the subjunctive. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it was not put in the subjunctive after the negation because of the similarity of the verse-endings, and both readings are permissible. End. This is not so, because the nominative, as we mentioned, is not a consequence but a clear conjunction, while the subjunctive makes it a consequence, so they differ. Abu al-Hajjaj al-A'lam held that a verb may be nominative while its meaning is that of the subjunctive after the fa', and this is rare. The grammarians only made the meaning of the nominative different from that of the subjunctive out of consideration for the majority of Arabic usage, and took this as their evidence. This verse is like the apparent sense of Ibn 'Atiyyah's words, and Ibn 'Usfur and others have refuted this.

﴿This is the Day of Judgement; We have gathered you﴾ — to the disbelievers — ﴿and the former peoples﴾: the people of Nuh, peace be upon him, and the other disbelievers whose time preceded the time of those addressed, i.e., We have gathered you for the separation between the happy and the wretched. ﴿So if you have any stratagem﴾: i.e., on this day, just as you had in the world schemes by which you plotted against the religion of Allah and His friends. ﴿Then use it against Me﴾ today. The reading of the majority is a repetition or an explanation of the destination. Ruways, on the authority of Ya'qub, read it with a fatha on the lam (inflected as a report), meaning: when they were commanded, they complied and set off, since it was not possible for them to delay, having become compelled to set off. ﴿With three branches﴾: 'Ata' said: it is the smoke of Jahannam. It was narrated that it rises from three places, and the disbelievers think that it will shield them from the Fire, so they rush toward it, only to find it in the worst condition. Ibn 'Abbas said: (p-407) it is said this to the worshippers of the cross: the believers are in the shade of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, while they are in the shade of their object of worship, which is the cross, which has three branches. A shi'b is that which separates from a single body. ﴿Neither shading﴾: a negation of the merits of shade. ﴿Nor availing﴾: i.e., nor will it avail them anything against the heat of the blaze. ﴿Indeed, it throws up sparks﴾: the pronoun in "innaha" refers to Jahannam. The majority read "bi-sharar," while 'Isa read "bi-shirar" with an alif between the two r's, and Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Miqsam likewise but with a kasra on the shin. This may be the plural of sharar, i.e., "with embers of punishment," or it may be an adjective placed in the position of its noun, i.e., "with evil ones of the people," as you say: "qawm shirar," the plural of sharr (not the elative form), and "qawm khiyar," the plural of khayr (not the elative form). This is feminized as "sharrah" and "khayrah" for the feminine, unlike when the two are used as elatives; they have rules mentioned in grammar. The majority read "kal-qasr" (as the fortress). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Hasan, and Ibn Miqsam read it with a fatha on the qaf and the sad. Ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan also read "ka-l-qisar," with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the sad. Some readers read it with a fatha on the qaf and a kasra on the sad. Ibn Mas'ud read it with a damma on both. "Therein are lions and leopards."

The explanation of most of these readings has already been given in the vocabulary section. The majority, among them 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), read "jimalat" with a kasra on the jim, with an alif and a ta', the plural of "jimal," which is the plural of jamal (camels). It is like their saying "rijalat Quraysh." Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, and Abu Raja', with a variant from them, read it the same way, except that they put a damma on the jim, and it means the ropes of ships. One unit of these is "jumlah," since it is a bundle (jumlah) of strengths and powers. Then it was pluralized as "jumal" and "jimal," then "jumal" was pluralized again as a sound plural, so they said "jumalat." It was also said: "jimalat" means the large cables of bridges. Ibn 'Abbas said: (p-407) it is said this to the worshippers of the cross: the believers are in the shade of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, while they are in the shade of their object of worship, which is the cross, which has three branches. A shi'b is that which separates from a single body. ﴿Neither shading﴾: a negation of the merits of shade. ﴿Nor availing﴾: i.e., nor will it avail them anything against the heat of the blaze. ﴿Indeed, it throws up sparks﴾: the pronoun in "innaha" refers to Jahannam. The majority read "bi-sharar," while 'Isa read "bi-shirar" with an alif between the two r's, and Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Miqsam likewise but with a kasra on the shin. This may be the plural of sharar, i.e., "with embers of punishment," or it may be an adjective placed in the position of its noun, i.e., "with evil ones of the people," as you say: "qawm shirar," the plural of sharr (not the elative form), and "qawm khiyar," the plural of khayr (not the elative form). This is feminized as "sharrah" and "khayrah" for the feminine, unlike when the two are used as elatives; they have rules mentioned in grammar. The majority read "kal-qasr" (as the fortress). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Hasan, and Ibn Miqsam read it with a fatha on the qaf and the sad. Ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan also read "ka-l-qisar," with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the sad. Some readers read it with a fatha on the qaf and a kasra on the sad. Ibn Mas'ud read it with a damma on both. It is as if it were a shortened form of "qusur" (palaces), just as they shortened "najm" and "namir" from "nujum" and "numur." The rajiz said:

"Therein are lions and leopards."

The explanation of most of these readings has already been given in the vocabulary section. The majority, among them 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), read "jimalat" with a kasra on the jim, with an alif and a ta', the plural of "jimal," which is the plural of jamal (camels). Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, and Abu Raja', with a variant from them, read it the same way, except that they put a damma on the jim, and it means the ropes of ships. Then it was pluralized as "jumal" and "jimal," then "jumal" was pluralized again as a sound plural, so they said "jumalat." It was also said: "jimalat" means the large cables of bridges. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, Abu 'Amr in the narration of al-Asma'i, and Harun on his authority read "jimalah" with a kasra on the jim, the ta' being attached to "jimal" to feminize the collective noun, like "hajar" and "hijarah." ﴿Proceed to that which you used to deny.﴾ ﴿Proceed to a shadow with three branches,﴾ ﴿neither shading nor availing against the blaze.﴾ ﴿Indeed, it throws up sparks like a fortress,﴾ ﴿as if they were yellow camels.﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿This is a day when they will not speak,﴾ ﴿nor will they be permitted to offer excuses.﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿This is the Day of Judgement; We have gathered you and the former peoples.﴾ ﴿So if you have any stratagem, then use it against Me.﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿Indeed, the God-conscious will be amid shades and springs,﴾ ﴿and fruits of what they desire.﴾ ﴿"Eat and drink with satisfaction for what you used to do."﴾ ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿"Eat and enjoy yourselves a little; indeed you are criminals."﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down.﴾ ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾ ﴿So in what statement after this will they believe?﴾

It is said to the deniers: ﴿Proceed to that which you used to deny﴾, i.e., of the punishment. ﴿Proceed to a shadow﴾: an imperative. The reading of the majority is a repetition or an explanation of the destination. Ruways, on the authority of Ya'qub, read it with a fatha on the lam (inflected as a report), meaning: when they were commanded, they complied and set off, since it was not possible for them to delay, having become compelled to set off. ﴿With three branches﴾: 'Ata' said: it is the smoke of Jahannam. It was narrated that it rises from three places, and the disbelievers think that it will shield them from the Fire, so they rush toward it, only to find it in the worst condition. Ibn 'Abbas said: (p-407) it is said this to the worshippers of the cross: the believers are in the shade of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, while they are in the shade of their object of worship, which is the cross, which has three branches. A shi'b is that which separates from a single body. ﴿Neither shading﴾: a negation of the merits of shade. ﴿Nor availing﴾: i.e., nor will it avail them anything against the heat of the blaze. ﴿Indeed, it throws up sparks﴾: the pronoun in "innaha" refers to Jahannam. The majority read "bi-sharar," while 'Isa read "bi-shirar" with an alif between the two r's, and Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Miqsam likewise but with a kasra on the shin. This may be the plural of sharar, i.e., "with embers of punishment," or it may be an adjective placed in the position of its noun, i.e., "with evil ones of the people," as you say: "qawm shirar," the plural of sharr (not the elative form), and "qawm khiyar," the plural of khayr (not the elative form). This is feminized as "sharrah" and "khayrah" for the feminine, unlike when the two are used as elatives; they have rules mentioned in grammar. The majority read "kal-qasr" (as the fortress). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Hasan, and Ibn Miqsam read it with a fatha on the qaf and the sad. Ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan also read "ka-l-qisar," with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the sad. Some readers read it with a fatha on the qaf and a kasra on the sad. Ibn Mas'ud read it with a damma on both. It is as if it were a shortened form of "qusur" (palaces), just as they shortened "najm" and "namir" from "nujum" and "numur." The rajiz said:

"Therein are lions and leopards."

The explanation of most of these readings has already been given in the vocabulary section. The majority, among them 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), read "jimalat" with a kasra on the jim, with an alif and a ta', the plural of "jimal," which is the plural of jamal (camels). It is like their saying "rijalat Quraysh." Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, and Abu Raja', with a variant from them, read it the same way, except that they put a damma on the jim, and it means the ropes of ships. One unit of these is "jumlah," since it is a bundle (jumlah) of strengths and powers. Then it was pluralized as "jumal" and "jimal," then "jumal" was pluralized again as a sound plural, so they said "jumalat." It was also said: "jimalat" means the large cables of bridges. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, Abu 'Amr in the narration of al-Asma'i, and Harun on his authority read "jimalah" with a kasra on the jim, the ta' being attached to "jimal" to feminize the collective noun, like "hajar" and "hijarah." Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sulami, al-A'mash, Abu Haywah, Abu Bahriyyah, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, and Ruways read likewise, except that they put a damma on the jim. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: "jimalat" are the large ropes of ships, which are their great cables; when they gather round, one against another, large masses result. Ibn 'Abbas also said: "jimalat" are large pieces of copper, and the derivation of these is from the name "jumlah." Al-Hasan read "sufr" with a damma on the fa', while the majority read it with a sukun. It likened the sparks first to the fortress, which is the castle in terms of size and in terms of height in the air, and second to camels, to clarify the comparison. Do you not see that they liken camels to large jars, which are palaces? The poet said:

"I halted there with my she-camel, and she was like a jar, so that I might fulfill the need of the one who lingers."

Whoever reads with a damma on the jim, the comparison is in terms of size and height. Bright yellow is more similar to the color of sparks. The majority said so. It was also said: "sufr sud" (yellowish-black), and it was said: "sud" inclining toward yellow. 'Imran ibn Hittan al-Raqashi said:

"They called to them with the highest of their voices and cast at them, like the camels of yellow color, that tear the skin."

Al-A'mash, al-A'raj, Zayd ibn 'Ali, 'Isa, Abu Haywah, and 'Asim in one narration read ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾ with a fatha on the mim, while the majority read it with a damma. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: when it is attached to a non-declinable noun, it is built, so the vowel is a building vowel, and it is in the position of a nominative. The author of al-Lawami' said: 'Isa said it is the dialect of lower Mudar, meaning that they built "yawm" with "la" on the fatha, because they made "yawm ma' la" like a single word, so it is in the position of the nominative, since it is the predicate of the subject. End. The sentence introduced by a present-tense verb, whether affirmative or negated, the Basrans do not allow building the adverb attached to it in any way; this is only a Kufan doctrine. The author of al-Lawami' said: it may also be a correct accusative as an adverb, so that this becomes a reference to what preceded in the speech, not a reference to "yawm," and the operator governing the accusative of "yawm" would be a call preceded by a description of (p-408) Jahannam and its throwing of sparks, in "the day when they will not speak," so "yawma'idhin" becomes an intervening clause that does not prevent the freeing of the operator for its object, just as in ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 47] ﴿Both having branches﴾ [al-Rahman: 48]. End. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it may also be an adverb, and the reference by "this" is to its throwing of sparks. al-Zamakhshari said: al-A'mash put it in the accusative, meaning: this which has been related to you occurs on that day. Here there is a negation of their speech, while Allah has informed us that they spoke at places during this day, and this is in consideration of the length of the day, so it is valid to negate speech in it at one time and affirm it at another, or the negation refers to speech with a proof that benefits, and their speech with what does not benefit is treated as no speech at all.

All the readers, as far as I know, read ﴿wa-la yu'dhanu﴾ in the passive. Abu 'Ali al-Ahwazi related that Zayd ibn 'Ali read "wa-la ya'dhanu" in the active, meaning Allah, Exalted is He. ﴿fa-ya'taddhirun﴾: it is conjoined to ﴿wa-la yu'dhanu﴾ and falls within the scope of the negation of permission, meaning: there is no permission, so there is no excuse-making, and he did not make the excuse-making a consequence of permission, so that it would be put in the subjunctive. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it was not put in the subjunctive after the negation because of the similarity of the verse-endings, and both readings are permissible. End. Thus he made the refusal of the subjunctive the similarity of verse-endings, and said both readings are permissible, and it appears from his words that the nominative and subjunctive are equal and their meaning is one. This is not so, because the nominative, as we mentioned, is not a consequence but a clear conjunction, while the subjunctive makes it a consequence, so they differ. Abu al-Hajjaj al-A'lam held that a verb may be nominative while its meaning is that of the subjunctive after the fa', and this is rare. The grammarians only made the meaning of the nominative different from that of the subjunctive out of consideration for the majority of Arabic usage, and took this as their evidence. This verse is like the apparent sense of Ibn 'Atiyyah's words, and Ibn 'Usfur and others have refuted this.

﴿This is the Day of Judgement; We have gathered you﴾ — to the disbelievers — ﴿and the former peoples﴾: the people of Nuh, peace be upon him, and the other disbelievers whose time preceded the time of those addressed, i.e., We have gathered you for the separation between the happy and the wretched. ﴿So if you have any stratagem﴾: i.e., on this day, just as you had in the world schemes by which you plotted against the religion of Allah and His friends. ﴿Then use it against Me﴾ today. This is a challenge to them and a rebuke. Since Surat al-Insan mentioned briefly some of the conditions of the disbelievers in the Hereafter and expanded on the description of the conditions of the believers there, this surah expands on the description of the disbelievers and is brief on the description of the believers, so that a balance was achieved between the two surahs. The majority read ﴿fi zilal﴾ as the plural of zill, while al-A'mash read "fi zulal," the plural of zullah. ﴿Eat and drink﴾: an address to them in the Hereafter, with the saying implied, indicated by ﴿for what you used to do﴾.

﴿Eat and enjoy yourselves﴾: an address to the disbelievers in the world. (A little): i.e., for a little time, since the utmost of your eating and enjoyment is death. It is an address of threat to whoever among Quraysh and others committed crime. ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down"﴾: whoever said this surah is Meccan said it was about Quraysh, and whoever said this verse is Medinan said it was about the hypocrites. He refused and said: "There is no good in a religion without prayer." The meaning of "bow down": be humble before Allah and submit to Him by accepting His revelation. It was also said: bowing here is an expression for prayer, and bowing was singled out from its acts because the Arabs used to be disdainful of bowing and prostration. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sulami, al-A'mash, Abu Haywah, Abu Bahriyyah, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, and Ruways read likewise, except that they put a damma on the jim. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: "jimalat" are the large ropes of ships, which are their great cables; when they gather round, one against another, large masses result. Ibn 'Abbas also said: "jimalat" are large pieces of copper, and the derivation of these is from the name "jumlah." Al-Hasan read "sufr" with a damma on the fa', while the majority read it with a sukun. It likened the sparks first to the fortress, which is the castle in terms of size and in terms of height in the air, and second to camels, to clarify the comparison. Do you not see that they liken camels to large jars, which are palaces? The poet said:

"I halted there with my she-camel, and she was like a jar, so that I might fulfill the need of the one who lingers."

Whoever reads with a damma on the jim, the comparison is in terms of size and height. Bright yellow is more similar to the color of sparks. The majority said so. It was also said: "sufr sud" (yellowish-black), and it was said: "sud" inclining toward yellow. 'Imran ibn Hittan al-Raqashi said:

"They called to them with the highest of their voices and cast at them, like the camels of yellow color, that tear the skin."

Al-A'mash, al-A'raj, Zayd ibn 'Ali, 'Isa, Abu Haywah, and 'Asim in one narration read ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾ with a fatha on the mim, while the majority read it with a damma. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: when it is attached to a non-declinable noun, it is built, so the vowel is a building vowel, and it is in the position of a nominative. The author of al-Lawami' said: 'Isa said it is the dialect of lower Mudar, meaning that they built "yawm" with "la" on the fatha, because they made "yawm ma' la" like a single word, so it is in the position of the nominative, since it is the predicate of the subject. End. The sentence introduced by a present-tense verb, whether affirmative or negated, the Basrans do not allow building the adverb attached to it in any way; this is only a Kufan doctrine. The author of al-Lawami' said: it may also be a correct accusative as an adverb, so that this becomes a reference to what preceded in the speech, not a reference to "yawm," and the operator governing the accusative of "yawm" would be a call preceded by a description of (p-408) Jahannam and its throwing of sparks, in "the day when they will not speak," so "yawma'idhin" becomes an intervening clause that does not prevent the freeing of the operator for its object, just as in ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 47] ﴿Both having branches﴾ [al-Rahman: 48]. End. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it may also be an adverb, and the reference by "this" is to its throwing of sparks. al-Zamakhshari said: al-A'mash put it in the accusative, meaning: this which has been related to you occurs on that day. Here there is a negation of their speech, while Allah has informed us that they spoke at places during this day, and this is in consideration of the length of the day, so it is valid to negate speech in it at one time and affirm it at another, or the negation refers to speech with a proof that benefits, and their speech with what does not benefit is treated as no speech at all.

All the readers, as far as I know, read ﴿wa-la yu'dhanu﴾ in the passive. Abu 'Ali al-Ahwazi related that Zayd ibn 'Ali read "wa-la ya'dhanu" in the active, meaning Allah, Exalted is He. ﴿fa-ya'taddhirun﴾: it is conjoined to ﴿wa-la yu'dhanu﴾ and falls within the scope of the negation of permission, meaning: there is no permission, so there is no excuse-making, and he did not make the excuse-making a consequence of permission, so that it would be put in the subjunctive. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it was not put in the subjunctive after the negation because of the similarity of the verse-endings, and both readings are permissible. End. Thus he made the refusal of the subjunctive the similarity of verse-endings, and said both readings are permissible, and it appears from his words that the nominative and subjunctive are equal and their meaning is one. This is not so, because the nominative, as we mentioned, is not a consequence but a clear conjunction, while the subjunctive makes it a consequence, so they differ. Abu al-Hajjaj al-A'lam held that a verb may be nominative while its meaning is that of the subjunctive after the fa', and this is rare. The grammarians only made the meaning of the nominative different from that of the subjunctive out of consideration for the majority of Arabic usage, and took this as their evidence. This verse is like the apparent sense of Ibn 'Atiyyah's words, and Ibn 'Usfur and others have refuted this.

﴿This is the Day of Judgement; We have gathered you﴾ — to the disbelievers — ﴿and the former peoples﴾: the people of Nuh, peace be upon him, and the other disbelievers whose time preceded the time of those addressed, i.e., We have gathered you for the separation between the happy and the wretched. ﴿So if you have any stratagem﴾: i.e., on this day, just as you had in the world schemes by which you plotted against the religion of Allah and His friends. ﴿Then use it against Me﴾ today. This is a challenge to them and a rebuke. Since Surat al-Insan mentioned briefly some of the conditions of the disbelievers in the Hereafter and expanded on the description of the conditions of the believers there, this surah expands on the description of the disbelievers and is brief on the description of the believers, so that a balance was achieved between the two surahs. The majority read ﴿fi zilal﴾ as the plural of zill, while al-A'mash read "fi zulal," the plural of zullah. ﴿Eat and drink﴾: an address to them in the Hereafter, with the saying implied, indicated by ﴿for what you used to do﴾.

﴿Eat and enjoy yourselves﴾: an address to the disbelievers in the world. (A little): i.e., for a little time, since the utmost of your eating and enjoyment is death. It is an address of threat to whoever among Quraysh and others committed crime. ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down"﴾: whoever said this surah is Meccan said it was about Quraysh, and whoever said this verse is Medinan said it was about the hypocrites. Muqatil said: it was revealed about Thaqif, who said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Remove the prayer from us, for we will not bow; it is a disgrace." He refused and said: "There is no good in a religion without prayer." The meaning of "bow down": be humble before Allah and submit to Him by accepting His revelation. It was also said: bowing here is an expression for prayer, and bowing was singled out from its acts because the Arabs used to be disdainful of bowing and prostration. In this surah, after every sentence, comes the statement: ﴿Woe that day to the deniers!﴾, because each sentence in it contains an account by Allah, Exalted is He, of matters of the conditions of the Hereafter and descriptions of matters of the conditions of this world, so it is fitting that we mention the threat after each sentence to the one who denies, with woe on the Day of the Hereafter. The pronoun in "ba'dahu" refers to the Qur'an, and the meaning is that it has contained, in terms of inimitability, eloquence, reports of unseen matters, and other things, what no divine book has contained. So if they deny it, then in what statement after it will they believe? I.e., it is not possible for them to believe any statement after they have denied this statement, which is the Qur'an. The majority read "yu'minun" with the third-person ya', while Ya'qub and Ibn 'Amir in one narration read it with the second-person ta'.
